notes.meaning: John sees a door standing open in heaven and hears the clear, trumpet-like voice of Jesus inviting him up. God calls him to see what will happen in the future, giving him a view of world events from heaven's perspective. It offers deep comfort by reminding believers that God rules over everything before troubles begin.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe the call to 'come up here' represents the rapture, where the church is caught up to heaven before the tribulation begins.

notes.meaning: Immediately, the Holy Spirit fills John with a powerful vision of heaven. He sees a glorious throne already set in place, with God the Father seated firmly upon it. This assures the church that God is never caught off guard and actively reigns over the entire universe.

Instead of describing God with human features, John describes his brilliance using sparkling gems like jasper and fiery carnelian. An emerald-green rainbow completely circles the throne. This shows that God's majestic rule and justice are always wrapped in his faithful mercy and covenant promises.

Around the main throne sit twenty-four elders on smaller thrones, dressed in white garments and wearing crowns of gold. They likely represent the whole body of God's redeemed people from both the Old and New Testaments. Their white robes and crowns show they share in the victory Christ won for them.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe the twenty-four elders are a special order of exalted angels rather than redeemed human beings.

notes.meaning: Flashes of lightning and rumblings of thunder come from the throne, echoing the awesome power God showed at Mount Sinai. In front of the throne burn seven torches of fire. These burning flames represent the full and perfect work of the Holy Spirit giving light and life.

differ.view: Some take the seven torches to be seven angels who serve before God's throne.

notes.meaning: In front of the throne lies a wide, peaceful floor that looks like a crystal-clear sea of glass. Surrounding the throne are four living creatures covered with eyes in front and back. Their many eyes show their sharp alertness and deep understanding as they serve God.

The four creatures look like a lion, an ox, a man, and a flying eagle. They highlight the finest qualities across God's earthly creation, representing strength, patient service, human wisdom, and swiftness. All of these noble qualities are brought together to honor and praise God.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: A long-standing traditional view identifies the four creatures as symbols of the four Gospel writers: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

notes.meaning: Each of the four creatures has six wings and never stops praising God day and night. They proclaim that the Lord God Almighty is completely holy, repeating the word three times to show his ultimate purity. They worship him as the eternal God who existed in the past, exists right now, and is coming again.

Whenever the living creatures give praise and thanks, the twenty-four elders immediately fall on their faces before the eternal King. They lay their golden crowns at the foot of the throne to show that all their victories come from God alone. True worship means gladly placing all our achievements under his feet.

The elders declare that the Lord God is worthy of all glory, honor, and power. He deserves total praise because he created everything in the universe out of nothing. Every creature exists and was brought into being simply because it pleased him.
